questions.q: What does "Shipped".strip() do to the string "  shipped \n"?
options: Removes the leading and trailing whitespace, including the newline
Converts it to uppercase
Deletes all letters from the string
Splits it into a list of characters
questions.explain: .strip() removes whitespace from both ends of a string, including newline characters.

options: A list: ['1002', '502', 'Marcus Ibeh']
A single string with commas removed
The number of commas in the string
A dictionary of key-value pairs
questions.explain: .split(sep) breaks a string into a list of substrings wherever the separator appears.

questions.q: After fields = raw_line.split(','), what type is fields[0] even if it looks like a number?
options: A string
An int
A float
A bool
questions.explain: Every piece produced by .split() is a string, regardless of what it looks like.

questions.q: What does the f-string f"Unit price: ${unit_price:.2f}" do when unit_price is 129.99?
options: Formats it as a float with exactly 2 decimal places: $129.99
Rounds it to the nearest whole dollar
Converts it to a string with no decimal places
Raises an error because f-strings can't contain format specifiers
questions.explain: :.2f is a format specifier that displays a float with exactly two decimal places.

questions.q: Why is manually splitting a line on commas fragile compared to using a real CSV reader (covered in Chapter 3)?
options: It breaks if any field itself contains a comma, like a name written 'Smith, Jane'
split(',') cannot handle numbers at all
It is fragile because it runs slower than any other method
There is no real difference; both approaches are equally robust
questions.explain: A proper CSV reader correctly handles commas inside quoted fields, which manual splitting cannot.
